Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Basic guessing rules Players will attempt to describe the concepts on the cards, using only the symbols on the board. Use the green question mark pawn to indicate the main thing being described, and green cubes to convey aspects of that thing. For example, to describe "milk", you could try: LIQUID ? + FOOD AND DRINK 🟩 + WHITE 🟩 To describe Vincent Van Gogh: MAN ? + ART/PAINT 🟩 + EAR 🟩 + CUT 🟩 You can use the coloured exclamation point pawns and their corresponding cubes to describe other aspects of your concept without your clues getting mixed up. For "Eiffel Tower", you could try: BUILDING ? + METAL 🟩 COUNTRY/FLAG ! + RED 🟥 + WHITE 🟥 + BLUE 🟥 Players here would know that the "red, white and blue" applied to the country or flag, not to the building itself. They'd also know that the thing they were trying to guess was the BUILDING. The clue-giver can remove pawns and cubes and move them around as much as they like, during their turn. Gameplay One player (or two, if the game is set to a larger team size) draw a card and choose a word or phrase to describe to the remaining players. Blue words are easy; red words are hard; grey words are challenging. There is no difference in scoring for the different groups, so choose what difficulty level the group wants to play at. The first player to guess the right answer wins 2VP, and the player (or duo) giving the clue win 1VP. The next player(s) around the table then give the next set of clues. If all guessers click "give up", the round ends with no points scored. But you're still allowed to make guesses after having given up. In a standard game: once twelve words have been guessed, the game ends. (If set to a "short game", this ends when each player has had one word guessed.) Casual play The original game notes that "During our extensive testing, we eventually abandoned the points system and kept only the pleasure of guessing and being guessed. Feel free to do the same as your enjoyment of the experience will be just as large!" - if you choose "no end" when setting up a game at BGA, it will continue forever. In Concept, your goal is to guess words through the association of icons. A team of two players – neighbors at the table – choose a word or phrase that the other players need to guess. Acting together, this team places pieces judiciously on the available icons on the game board.

To get others to guess "milk", for example, the team might place the question mark icon (which signifies the main concept) on the liquid icon, then cubes of this color on the icons for "food/drink" and "white". For a more complicated concept, such as "Leonardo DiCaprio", the team can use the main concept and its matching cubes to clue players into the hidden phrase being an actor or director, while then using sub-concept icons and their matching cubes to gives clues to particular movies in which DiCaprio starred, such as Titanic or Inception.

The first player to discover the word or phrase receives 2 victory points, the team receives points as well, and the player who ends up with the most points wins.
community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] This is one of a zillion pseudo-charades games, and not a  good one.   The dealio here is the use of an image board to communicate cues from cards instead of acting things out as in basic charades or drawing things (Pictionary, etc) or using limited words (Taboo, Password, 25 Words or Less) or whatnot. The imageboard manages to be both too big to communicate things clearly and yet too limited to have the sort of clues you want. That might be excusable if the images were either a bit more intuitive or if the reference sheet was not horrible. It's formatted different than the board for exactly n

[Rating: 1/10] A fun activity, but it's not a game. Even the authors say that playing without the (horrible IMO) scoring system is better. Then why did they put it in the game?

[Rating: 1/10] Boring, that's the best thing that I can say about this game. Here, use these abstract symbols, try and get people to guess something that's specific on the card you drew, and you can weight it so that something is more important, you can say that this is the most important concept, and for a party type game, it's just a party killer. It seemed cooler watching it on Table Top with Wil Wheaton, but playing it in real life, it's a snooze fest.

[Rating: 1/10] Party game where you have to get people to think of a word or phrase by giving picture clues from a board of choices.  Kind of a mix of Deception Hong Kong and Taboo/Charades/etc.

[Rating: 1.6/10] On a peu être joué avec des regles approximative mais c'est super brouillon et braillard. Un mauvais party game.  Edit : si en fait y'a pas de règles c'est normal ...

[Rating: 2/10] So many better options in this genre. Dixit, One Key, Mysterium, Pictures. All more intuitive and easier to pick up for non gamers than the smorgasboard of options here that are somehow too open but also too confined.

[Rating: 2/10] From Shire Games  Cackety Cack Cack McCack!  Shite hole of a 'game'  Luckily still a popular game so easily sold on.

[Rating: 2/10] Feels more like a concept for a game.  Some cards are ridiculously unbalanced compared to others, and my groups have decided to scrap the "rules" and make up our own since the creators did a terrible job.  With a better rulebook, and replacement cards ... I'd probably give this game a passing grade.

[Rating: 2/10] Terrible game, avoid it. Puzzling to put down the cubes, discussions in the process, then it's just a guessing game. If I would have play this genre again, I'd rather play Dixit, which is much smoother.

[Rating: 2/10] If you're with two, just play Imagine. If you're with more than that, play literally any other game. I only barely consider this an actual game instead of just an activity.

[Rating: 2/10] Concept is already the type of game I'm not interested in playing, but beyond that I just didn't find it very well designed.  Some friends and I finally tried to do a play session but we ended up being underwhelmed.  It's not deep, or satisfying, in my opinion
